content: Patients who are classified as chronic cases are highly likely to have tuberculosis caused by multidrug-resistant (MDR) organisms. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends susceptibility testing and the use of a tailored treatment regimen based on second-line drugs if such testing and drugs are available. However, the International Union Against Tuberculosis and Lung Disease (IUATLD) does not address this issue. Neither the WHO nor the IUATLD recommends baseline or follow-up biochemical testing. Instead, patients should be educated to recognize symptoms of drug toxicity and report them promptly. A new drug, bedaquiline, was approved by the FDA in December 2012 for the treatment of multidrug-resistant tuberculosis. In 2011, approximately 12 million people worldwide had tuberculosis, with about 630,000 cases being multidrug-resistant. Bedaquiline is intended for use primarily in cases of multidrug-resistant tuberculosis and extensively drug-resistant tuberculosis. Multidrug-resistant tuberculosis is defined as cases that do not respond to at least two of the four primary (first-line) antibiotics, which were developed in the 1950s and 1960s. However, bedaquiline carries a black-box warning due to its potential to cause arrhythmias, which may lead to cardiac arrest. A novel three-drug anti-tuberculosis regimen, known as PaMZ, has shown promise in recent studies. This regimen includes PA-824 (a nitroimidazooxazine), moxifloxacin (a fluoroquinolone), and pyrazinamide (a first-line TB drug). Results from a recent Phase II clinical trial published in The Lancet demonstrated that this regimen killed over 99% of tuberculosis bacteria within two weeks of treatment. New antituberculosis drugs are urgently needed for three main reasons: to shorten or simplify treatment for drug-susceptible tuberculosis, to improve treatment for drug-resistant tuberculosis, and to provide more effective treatment for latent tuberculosis infections. Currently, no truly novel compounds with significant potential impact on tuberculosis treatment are close to clinical trials. However, further research is warranted to optimize the effectiveness of once-weekly rifapentine regimens, particularly by using higher doses or combining rifapentine with moxifloxacin. Promising new drug categories for tuberculosis treatment include nitroimidazopyrans and oxazolidinones. Experimental data also suggest that drugs targeting the enzyme isocitrate lyase, which is thought to be essential for maintaining latent tuberculosis, may be useful for treating latent infections. Several other interventions have been proposed to improve treatment outcomes, though none have undergone rigorous clinical testing. These include innovative drug delivery systems, cytokine inhibitors, administration of protective cytokines such as interferon-gamma and interleukin-2, and nutritional supplements, particularly vitamin A and zinc. Research is also needed to identify factors that predict the risk of relapse, which would help determine the optimal length of treatment and enable more efficient allocation of resources for treatment supervision. Additionally, identifying behavioral factors that predict adherence to therapy could improve the use of directly observed therapy (DOT).
